hints: Picture the Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies and remember that the top of the peak marks the most probable energy.
When temperature rises the whole curve flattens and shifts to the right, so the height of that peak must fall.
The total area under the curve stays the same for a fixed sample, so if the peak gets lower the tail out at high energy must get fatter.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Boltzmann distribution**

Think of a plot of number of molecules against energy. It starts at zero, rises quickly to a peak, then tails off slowly.

The peak energy is the most probable energy, $E_{mp}$, and the total area under the curve equals the total number of molecules.

**See what higher temperature does to the peak**

Heating gives molecules more kinetic energy on average, so the distribution spreads out over a wider range of energies.

Because the same number of molecules is now spread more widely, the peak becomes lower and moves slightly to the right. So the number with the most probable energy decreases.

**See what higher temperature does to the high energy tail**

With more total energy available, a larger fraction of molecules can reach high energies well to the right of the peak.

The curve flattens but its tail lifts up, so the number of molecules with higher energy increases. Lower peak plus fatter high energy tail matches decreases then increases.

options.A: Half right and half wrong. The peak height does decrease, but the high energy tail does not decrease. Heating pushes more molecules to high energy, so this second part is opposite to the true effect.
options.B: Exactly right. Higher temperature spreads the distribution, so the peak is lower (fewer molecules have the most probable energy) and the tail at high energy is higher (more molecules have higher energy).
options.C: Back to front. Students sometimes think a hotter sample means more molecules crowd at the peak value. In fact the peak gets lower and shifts right, and heating increases, not decreases, the number at high energy.
options.D: The high energy part is correct, it increases, but the peak part is wrong. The peak cannot get taller on heating because the fixed total number of molecules is spread over a wider energy range, so the maximum must fall.
